sections.name: Globalization Current Issues & Cross-Cultural Perspectives
sections.notes: This Writing 150 thematic will promote the development of strong writing and critical reasoning skills by providing students an opportunity to examine those values, belief systems, and ideologies that affect every dimension of our lives, whether personal, social, professional, or civic. We will approach writing as a recursive process of engaged reading, invention, arrangement, revision, and editing. The texts we produce will demonstrate respect for the needs of readers and will exemplify the kind of ethical rhetoric that has the potential to engage with and influence the worlds values and belief systems in positive ways.

sections.name: AI Writing Lab
sections.notes: AI Intensive.This project-based course emphasizes experimentation and reflection. Each week, instructors will challenge students to put a diverse range of AI tools - including agentic AI - to the test. Activities and assignments will interrogate foundational assumptions about AI, knowledge generation, language, rhetoric, and the potential for humanistic inquiry. By working both with and against AI, students will hone their writing and critical-thinking skills while reflecting deeply on their engagement with these tools.

sections.name: Inside-Out Writing Workshop
sections.notes: Please allow 90 minutes of travel time before and after the listed course time. This course is being offered in conjunction with the USC Dornsife Prison Education Project. This class aims to create opportunities for USC and students in-custody to learn from each other in a rigorous and collaborative environment. This course will focus on autobiography, and each week, students will be tasked with drafting a new chapter of their life stories. We will try to understand ourselves and our society through reading, writing, with an emphasis on writing as a process. Work between USC and students in-custody will be exchanged via electronic correspondence or in person, dependent upon the facility. For D-clearance please email Professor DeDominic at dedomini@usc.edu.

sections.name: Community-Engaged Writing
sections.notes: Community-Engaged Writing provides upper-level students with advanced pre-professional training in analytical and argumentative writing in community-engaged contexts and builds skills applicable to a range of community-engaged careers after college. Students will participate in valuable networking opportunities with industry professionals and gain hands-on practical experience as they work with community partners to develop an in-depth capstone project. For D-clearance email professor Michelle Meyers meyersmi@usc.edu

sections.name: Writing in Practical Contexts
sections.notes: For information on this course, please email Professor Antonio Elefano at elefano@usc.edu. Please note that students must have completed (or currently be enrolled in) either WRIT 340 or CORE 112 as a prerequisite for this course. This course examines how being humorous allows authors and comics to tackle subjects in their work that might otherwise seem taboo, and how this freedom provides a unique opportunity for social commentary and critique. One particular emphasis is understanding how comedic authors balance the need to entertain an audience with their efforts to provide insight on controversial issues. Throughout the semester students will explore aspects of writing and argumentation by analyzing a range of comedic texts, and will have the opportunity to produce original work in a variety of comedic genres (rants; scripts; stand-up routines; sketches; etc.).
